question: In Italy non-scheduled public transport, including taxis and private hire vehicle (PHVs), is regulated by Law 21/1992, as updated by Decree-Law 135/2018 and Law 12/2019. This legislation provides for different penalties for similar infractions: taxi drivers, who are covered by Article 86 of the Highway Code, can be fined between EUR 86 and EUR 338.

PHV drivers however, falling as they do under Article 85, are subject to the same penalties but also risk losing their vehicle registration card and operations licence for between two and eight months.

There are significant differences in their tax obligations and administrative requirements: PHV drivers must provide tax documentation for each service they provide and complete a service logbook with details such as passenger name, date, departure and arrival address, and keep the logbook for at least 15 days. This could constitute a breach of the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR).
Taxi drivers, on the other hand, are under no such obligations, with payments often made in cash with no need to use the meter for journeys. Can the Commission therefore say: 1.
Whether it is aware of these legislative divergences and whether it believes them to constitute a potential distortion of the single market, which could favour taxi drivers to the detriment of PHVs?
Whether it considers these regulations to discriminate between these professional categories, with disproportionate penalties that could restrict the freedom to do business?
Whether it believes action to be needed to remedy these discrepancies, also in view of the need to comply with data privacy rules?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (26.6.2024) It is important that the rules are in line with EU law, notably the freedom of establishment (Article 49 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union).

The Commission clarified the limits Member States need to observe when regulating the sector in its Notice on well-functioning and sustainable local passenger transport-on-demand (taxis and Private Hire Vehicles (PHV))1.

When assessing different rules on local transport-on-demand (taxis and PHVs), it should be taken into account that according to Article 51(1) of the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union, the provisions of the Charter – including the freedom to conduct a business enshrined in Article 16 of the Charter – are addressed to the Member States only when they are implementing Union law.

The Commission believes that Member States will be attentive to the above-mentioned Notice when designing new rules, taking into account also the recent case law of the Court of Justice of the European Union. The Commission will continue to monitor the market, and reserves its right to update the Notice, if deemed necessary.

With regard to the compatibility of data protection and privacy rules with Italian law, Regulation (EU) 2016/6792 (General Data Protection Regulation) provides that any law laying down an obligation to collect personal data must meet an objective of public interest and be proportionate to the legitimate aim pursued.

The Constitutional Court of Italy examined the proportionality of the obligation to keep a detailed duty roster (work sheet) established by Article 11 (4) of the amended Italian law 21/1992 on non-scheduled public transport in point 5.6.1 of its judgement 56/2000 of 25 February 2020.
1 OJ C 62, 4.2.2022, p. 1. 2 Regulation (EU) 2016/679 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 27 April 2016 on the protection of
natural persons with regard to the processing of personal data and on the free movement of such data, and repealing Directive 95/46/EC (Text with EEA relevance), OJ L 119, 4.5.2016, p. 1–88.
